transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dave Mattingly.
President Trump says US and Iranian officials met for about three hours yesterday on the
sidelines of the UN General Assembly meeting in New York.
No major breakthroughs were announced, and the president offered few details about the
talks.
The meeting occurred shortly after Trump threatened to annihilate Iran if an agreement isn't
soon reached to end the war.
This week will mark seven months since the US and Israel began attacking Iran.
President Trump met with South Korea's president on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
NPR's Anthony Kuhn says the two discussed plans by Seoul for major investments in the
US.
South Korea's industry ministry briefed lawmakers on the first projects in a deal to invest
$350 billion in the US in exchange for lower tariffs.
They include a gas-fired power plant in Ensenal, Texas, which could help fuel new semiconductor
plants and AI data centers in the state.
They also include the building of up to eight nuclear reactors in the US and a liquid natural
gas project in Alaska.
Announcement of the projects came after lengthy negotiations by the two governments, which
still have to approve the plans.
Trump also reaffirmed his commitment to re-engaging diplomatically with North Korea, although
Pyongyang has repeatedly rejected his efforts at outreach.
Anthony Kuhn, NPR News, Seoul.
OpenAI is calling for the US to lead the way in establishing global safety standards for
artificial intelligence.
NPR's John Ruich says the company's CEO, Sam Altman, is scheduled to brief the UN Security
Council today, along with the head of Anthropic.
OpenAI is releasing its proposal at a time of intense debate about how to regulate artificial
intelligence after a string of incidents that have raised concern about the technology.
It says international safety and security standards are key to answering the question,
what does good look like in the mitigation of catastrophic AI risk?
AI companies and labs have to take accountability for developing AI safely, it says, but standards
will help more stakeholders have a say in how AI evolves.
OpenAI says the United States should lead an effort with other countries to develop
technical standards for the most cutting-edge artificial intelligence, including for recursive
self-improvement, or AI-building AI, which many believe could lead to the technology
spiraling out of human control.
John Ruich, NPR News.
Hurricane Polo has intensified to what forecasters are calling an extremely dangerous storm as
it spins off the coast of southwestern Mexico.
Polo is a Category 4 storm with top sustained winds of 155 miles per hour.
It was a Category 5 until moments ago.
The National Hurricane Center in Florida says Polo is expected to remain offshore but will
bring heavy rains and strong winds to the region.
Currently, that storm is almost stationary in the Pacific.
This is NPR News.
Heavy rains are falling across much of New Mexico this morning where flood watches are
in effect statewide.
The National Weather Service says flash flooding is likely from rain that could fall at a rate
of one to two inches per hour.
Forecasters say flooding is also possible in far west Texas.
They warn the heavy rains could trigger debris flows and areas burned by wildfires.
The rainy weather in that region is expected through tomorrow.
The Trump administration says it's canceling the health insurance for 760,000 phantom enrollees
on healthcare.gov.
As NPR's Selena Simmons-Duffin reports, the government is providing few details about
how it determined the health plans were not legitimate.
Trump administration officials explained in a press conference that they suspected "fraudster
brokers" had signed up people who weren't eligible or who didn't even know they had
been signed up.
The fight against fraudulent brokers has been going on for years, says Cynthia Cox of the
nonprofit health research organization KFF, but she questioned this approach.
"There could have been collateral damage here."
If someone didn't file a claim, she points out, they might have just been healthy, and
if they didn't respond to the notice in time, they might have just missed it.
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services did not respond to NPR's questions by airtime
about what happens if there were mistakes and people had their plans cancelled in error.
Selena Simmons-Duffin, NPR News, Washington.
For the first time in 15 years, Princeton University has fallen from the top spot on
U.S. News and World Report's rankings of colleges and universities.
MIT is now number one, Princeton drops to number two.
I'm Dave Mattingly in Washington.
